text:
San Jose was completed by William Campbell and his brother, Thomas, in May of 1847. The boundaries of this first effort were Market and eighth on the west and east respectively, and Julian and Reed on the north and south. A second survey was completed in May of 1848 by C. S. Lyman. Lyman extended the town limits to eleventh street on the east. A third survey in 1850 established the eastern boundary of the city at Coyote Creek and the western boundary 660 feet west of the Guadalupe River. At this time the city limits, on a northwest-southeast axis, were three miles long (Foote 1888, Hall 1871). As time passed, lands surrounding this initial city core were acquired and streets laid out to serve increased population demands. By 1888, the city limits extended north to Hedding Street and south to Alma Avenue (Foote, 1888).
The gold rush of 1848 almost emptied San Jose and the Santa Clara Valley of inhabitants. Soon, however, thousands of persons were passing through San Jose on their way to the gold fields and a new growth and expansion of the town was assured. Not only did San Jose become a vigorous trade center, but it was also made the capital of California. The first duly elected state legislature met in San Jose on December 15, 1849. Four days after convening, a bill was introduced to move the capital to Monterey. This was apparently the result of dissatisfaction over the fact that the State House was not ready for occupancy by the total legislature. Accomodations for the members of the legislature were also deemed poor. This particular bill soon died after one reading. It was not long, however, before a new move to change the location of the capital was made in April, 1850, by General Mariano Guadelupe Vallejo. Vallejo, naturally, wanted the capital moved to Vallejo and was quick to point out the obvious advantages of such a move. Vallejo sweetened the pot with offers of land an financial assistance for the construction of a new State House. After much opposition and delay, Vallejo's forces were victorious in their efforts and an act providing for the removal of the capital to Vallejo was carried out on May 1, 1851 (Sawyer 1922; Winther 1935).
The setback caused by the removal of the capital was only temporary. Three thousand people were now residing in and around San Jose by 1851 and the city was continuing to expand. As the result of an Act passed by the legislature on March 27, 1850, San Jose had become incorporated and the city had soon established a government consisting of a mayor and seven councilmen. This form of government was retained until 1916 when San Jose adopted the commission form of government (Sawyer 1922; Winther 1935).
